title: DynamoDB single-table design and transactions
goal: By the end, you can explain how one DynamoDB request can return a whole account screen, give the same records a second address for questions that don't know the account, and move money between two accounts so that every change happens or none does.
opening:
You split a dinner bill with a friend, and later you send her your half, 30.00, from the payments app. The app keeps its records in DynamoDB, a database that Amazon runs for you on its own computers. To move the money, the app sends two requests: one takes 30.00 off your balance, and one adds 30.00 to hers.

One evening the app crashes between the two. Your balance is 30.00 lower, and hers hasn't moved.

It's easy to think that two changes sent a moment apart belong together, because in the code they sit side by side. But the database never sees the code. It sees two requests, and it saves each one on its own.

Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics read one account's newest payments with one request, and changed one record at a time. In this lesson, we'll fit a whole account screen into one request, give the same records a second address, and make the 30.00 move all at once or not at all. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments app moves 30.00 from your account to a friend's with two separate requests to DynamoDB. The first takes 30.00 off your balance. The second adds 30.00 to hers. The app crashes after the first request and before the second. What does the database hold now?
options: Neither change: the database notices that the second request never came, and undoes the first
Only the first change: each request is saved on its own, and nothing ties the two together
Both changes: the database finishes the second request when the app starts again
Neither change, as long as both requests carried the same transfer number
warmup.why: Each request changes one record, and DynamoDB saves it the moment the request succeeds. DynamoDB has no idea the two requests belong together, so the first change stays and the second never happens: 30.00 leaves your account and arrives nowhere. Nothing waits for the second request, and nothing replays it later. A shared transfer number can stop the same request from running twice, but it can't undo a request that already ran. A group of changes that happen together or not at all is called a transaction, and DynamoDB's is `TransactWriteItems`, in the third section.

sections.h: One request for the whole account screen: single-table design
sections.body:
Let's start with the screen you see before you send the money. The account screen in the payments app shows two things: your balance and your 20 newest payments. We want it to load with one request, because every request is a trip over the network. Model the access patterns first wrote down the six questions this app asks, called access patterns, and numbered them AP1 to AP6. The account screen is AP1.

First, a few words that DynamoDB uses. A table holds items, and an item is one record: a set of named values called attributes, such as `amountMinor` or `currency`. (Amounts are in minor units, cents, so 3000 means 30.00.) Every item has a primary key, the value DynamoDB finds it by, in two parts. The partition key decides where the item is stored. The sort key puts in order the items that share a partition key. Those items are kept together, sorted by sort key, and the group is called an item collection. A Query is the request that reads one unbroken run of one item collection, forward or backward.

In a SQL database such as PostgreSQL, the screen would be one query with a join. A join combines rows from two tables that share a value, here the account's row and its payment rows. DynamoDB has no joins. So let's build the screen up, one version at a time.

Version 1 copies the SQL layout. There's an `accounts` table keyed by account id, and a `payments` table with partition key `accountId` and sort key `createdAt`, the time of the payment. The screen needs a GetItem (a read of one item by its full key) on the first table and a Query on the second. That's two requests where SQL needed one, and every new screen adds more. The payment page wants the payment and its refunds: a third table and two more requests. The statement page, the list of money in and out, wants a fourth.

Version 2 puts every kind of item in one table. The key attributes get plain names, `pk` and `sk`, because they hold different things for different items. Your account's own item, its payments, its refunds and its ledger entries (one line each on your statement) all get the same partition key, `ACCT#A-1001`. Now they're one item collection, stored together and sorted by sort key. Alex DeBrie, an author who writes about DynamoDB, calls this pre-joining: you store the result of the join instead of working it out on every read. Each item also carries a `type` attribute, so your code knows what came back.

Picture a filing cabinet with one drawer per account. The drawer is the item collection, and the labels on the folders are the sort keys. The drawer keeps its folders in the order of their labels, and nothing else counts. It has no idea which folder is "the account". So the labels you choose decide what sits next to what.

Version 3 names the sort keys so that their order answers the question. DynamoDB compares sort keys one byte, about one character, at a time, so capital letters sort in alphabet order. The collection reads `LEDGER#...`, then `PAY#...`, then the account item, then `REFUND#...`. In Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics, the account item's sort key was `META`, and `M` sorts before `P`. Read the collection backward to get the newest payments first, and you'd meet the account item last, after every payment. So rename it `PROFILE`. `PA` sorts before `PR`, which puts the profile right after the newest payment. One Query, `sk BETWEEN "PAY#" AND "PROFILE"`, read backward with `Limit 21`, returns the profile and then the 20 newest payments. The stepper shows it, and two more questions that the same collection answers.

**A single table is a set of item collections whose sort keys you name on purpose, so that each screen is one unbroken run.** That's the picture for this lesson, and the next sections add to it.

The screen now costs one request. DynamoDB charges for reads in read units. A strongly consistent read, one that's sure to see every write that has finished, costs one unit per 4 KB. A Query adds up the sizes of the items it reads and rounds up to the next 4 KB. So 21 items of about 300 bytes, about 6.3 KB, cost 2 read units. DeBrie argues for this design, and he's plain about what it buys. The main win is fewer requests; the savings from running fewer tables are small. The price is a table that, in his words, looks "more like machine code than a simple spreadsheet". You can't read it without the key design next to it.

Two of the app's questions don't fit this drawer at all. Next, we'll see why, and give the same items a second address.

sections.h: A second address for the same items: global secondary indexes
sections.body:
Two of the access patterns can't use the account drawer. AP2 is the support desk: a customer reads a payment number off a receipt, and support looks it up. AP3 is a shop's dashboard: shop M-0042's FAILED payments between 09:00 and 12:00. (The code calls a shop a merchant, so its id is `merchantId`.) Neither question knows the account, so neither can name the partition key. The only other way in is a Scan, which reads every item in the table.

Model the access patterns first gave the answer: a second copy of the data, filed under a different key. Picture a second filing cabinet, kept by a clerk who photocopies every payment into a drawer per shop. In DynamoDB, the second cabinet is a global secondary index, or GSI. You create one by naming the attributes that form its partition key and its sort key. DynamoDB copies every item that has those attributes into the index, grouped and sorted by them. After every write to the table, it updates the copy. This table has two:

- `byPayment`, partition key `paymentId`, sort key `sk`. Payments and refunds both carry `paymentId`, and `PAY#` sorts before `REFUND#`. So one Query for `pay-81723` returns the payment, then its refunds in time order. That's AP2 and AP6, the refunds of a payment, in one request.
- `byMerchant`, partition key `merchantId`, sort key `status` then `createdAt`. AP3 fixes the shop and the status with `=` and asks for a range of `createdAt`.

That second index uses a feature DynamoDB added in November 2025. A GSI key can be built from up to four attributes for the partition key and four for the sort key. Before that, you glued two values into one extra attribute, such as `FAILED#2026-11-07T09:40:27Z`, and kept it in step with `status` yourself (and hoped nobody forgot).

The sort key is used from left to right, with no gaps, the rule from Model the access patterns first. A phone book works the same way. It's sorted by surname, then first name, so every Ann Smith sits on one run of pages, while finding every Ann means reading the whole book. Here the items are sorted by status first. "FAILED since 09:00" is one run, and "any status since 09:00" is scattered over every status. DynamoDB enforces the rule: ask for `createdAt > 09:00` without `status`, and it refuses the Query (the demo below prints the error). One more snag: `status` is a reserved word, one that DynamoDB keeps for its own use in the conditions you write. The condition must call it `#status` and say what that stands for in `expressionAttributeNames`.

An item that lacks an index's key attributes isn't in that index. Profiles, ledger entries and claims have no `merchantId`, so `byMerchant` holds payments and nothing else. That's called a sparse index, and you can use it on purpose: give an attribute only to the items you want listed.

The copies aren't free, and they lag. A payment has the key attributes of both indexes, so one PutItem, the write of one whole item, becomes three writes, and DynamoDB charges for each. It updates a GSI asynchronously: a moment after the write, not as part of it, the way the clerk photocopies a little after you file. So a payment written a moment ago can be missing from the shop's dashboard briefly. And you can't ask a GSI for a strongly consistent read at all. DynamoDB answers "Consistent reads are not supported on global secondary indexes". Reads that must see every write, such as the balance check before a transfer, go to the table.

That balance check matters, because the transfer from the opening touches two drawers at once. Next, we'll make its writes happen together.

sections.h: Moving money: five writes that happen together or not at all
sections.body:
Back to the opening. A transfer of 30.00 from A-1001 to A-2002 is five writes in this table. It takes 30.00 off A-1001's PROFILE item, a debit, and adds 30.00 to A-2002's, a credit. It puts one `LEDGER#` item into each account's collection, so both statements show the transfer. And it claims the transfer's idempotency key. That's a value the app makes once for each transfer and sends again on every retry. The claim is an item that says "this key has been used", so a retry can't move the money twice; Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics built it. The two accounts have different partition keys, so their items can sit on different machines. Let's build the transfer up.

Version 1 sends five separate requests. Each one is atomic for its own item: it happens completely or not at all. That promise covers nothing else. Stop the app after the debit, and 30.00 has left A-1001 and arrived nowhere, the crash from the opening. A retry can't tell which of the five steps already ran.

Version 2 sends one `BatchWriteItem`, a request that carries many writes. That saves trips over the network, but it promises nothing as a unit. The DynamoDB docs say that some of a batch's writes can succeed while others fail. It also can't update an item or check a condition. It can only put and delete whole items.

Version 3 is `TransactWriteItems`. A group of writes that happen together or not at all is called a transaction, and this is DynamoDB's. **DynamoDB applies every action in the request, or none of them.** One request carries up to 100 actions on up to 100 different items. They can be in several tables, all in the same AWS account and the same Region. AWS, Amazon Web Services, is the part of Amazon that runs DynamoDB, and a Region is one of its groups of data centres (there's one in Ireland, for example). The whole request can be at most 4 MB. An action is a Put, an Update, a Delete or a ConditionCheck. Each one can carry a condition: a test that DynamoDB checks against the item, in the same step as the write. Here are the debit and the claim. The credit and the two ledger puts go between them:

```kotlin
val debit = TransactWriteItem.builder().update(
    Update.builder().tableName(table)
        .key(Keys.key("ACCT#A-1001", "PROFILE"))
        .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt")
        .conditionExpression("balanceMinor >= :amt")          // no overdraft
        .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":amt" to Keys.n(3_000)))
        .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD)
        .build()
).build()
val claim = TransactWriteItem.builder().put(
    Put.builder().tableName(table)
        .item(Keys.key("IDEMP#k-1", "IDEMP") + mapOf("transferId" to Keys.s("txf-k-1")))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)")      // first use of this key only
        .build()
).build()
ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems(debit, credit, ledgerFrom, ledgerTo, claim) }
```

The debit's condition, `balanceMinor >= :amt`, means "only if the balance covers it". The claim's, `attribute_not_exists(pk)`, means "only if no item with this key exists yet". If any condition is false, nothing is written. The SDK, the library Amazon provides for calling DynamoDB from code, throws `TransactionCanceledException`. Its `cancellationReasons()` holds one entry per action, in the order you sent them. An action that was fine says `None`, and the one that failed says why, such as `ConditionalCheckFailed`. With `ALL_OLD` on an action, its reason also carries the item as it was. So the debit's reason shows the balance it failed on, and an empty item means the account doesn't exist.

You may be thinking, "Why a condition? I could read the balance first and check it in Kotlin." Picture two transfers from A-1001 at the same moment. Both read 100.00, both pass the check, and both write 70.00. One debit is lost. Putting that write in a transaction doesn't help, because the read happened outside it. The condition is checked against the item as it is when the transaction runs, in the same step as the change. And the update expression, `SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt`, does the sum on DynamoDB's side, so no out-of-date number from your code is ever written.

One more rule catches people: a transaction can't touch one item twice, so a transfer from A-1001 to A-1001 is refused.

The same tool closes the gap that Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics left open. There, the claim and the payment were two writes, and a crash between them left a claim with no payment. The worked example below puts both into one transaction. A transaction isn't free, though, and it promises less than you might expect. Next, we'll count what it costs.

steps: Read `TransferDemo.kt`. `transferActions` builds the five actions, and `main` sends three transfers: 30.00 with key `k-1`, 500.00 with key `k-2`, then `k-1` again.
A-1001 starts with 100.00. For each transfer, predict: does it commit, which action's reason is not `None`, and what are the balances afterwards?

```text
before: A-1001 10000, A-2002 5000; A-1001 ledger entries: 2
transfer 30.00 with key k-1: committed
  balances: A-1001 7000, A-2002 8000; A-1001 ledger entries: 3
transfer 500.00 with key k-2: TransactionCanceledException
  [0] debit A-1001   ConditionalCheckFailed
  [1] credit A-2002  None
  [2] ledger A-1001  None
  [3] ledger A-2002  None
  [4] claim          None
  balances: A-1001 7000, A-2002 8000; A-1001 ledger entries: 3
retry of k-1: TransactionCanceledException
  [0] debit A-1001   None
  [1] credit A-2002  None
  [2] ledger A-1001  None
  [3] ledger A-2002  None
```

Amounts are in cents. The first transfer writes all five items. The second fails only the debit's condition, and yet the credit, both ledger entries and the claim are missing too: nothing was written. The retry of `k-1` would have had the money (70.00 left), but its claim already exists, so the whole transaction is cancelled and nothing moves twice. The reasons come back in the order the actions were sent, which is how your code tells these cases apart.

aside.title: Is DynamoDB the Dynamo from the first lesson?
aside.body: Only in part. Why other data models exist met Dynamo, a design Amazon described in 2007, where any copy of the data takes writes and the copies may disagree for a while. DynamoDB, which Amazon opened to customers in 2012, kept the name and the idea of turning each key into a number, a hash, to spread the data over machines. But each of its partitions has one leader copy that puts the writes in order. That's what lets DynamoDB offer strongly consistent reads, conditions and the transactions in this section. So don't carry Dynamo's habits, such as merging two versions of a record after the fact, over to DynamoDB.

sections.h: What a transaction costs, and what it doesn't promise
sections.body:
The transfer in the last Try-it wrote five items. On a real DynamoDB bill, it costs as much as ten. DynamoDB charges for writes in write units, one for each item of up to 1 KB. A transaction costs twice what the same writes cost alone, because DynamoDB does two writes underneath for every item in it, one to prepare and one to commit. So the five-item transfer, every item under 1 KB, uses 10 write units instead of 5. It still uses them when it's cancelled. DynamoDB Local doesn't imitate this in the `ConsumedCapacity` it reports, so take the number from the AWS docs, not from the demo.

Transactions also collide. If two transactions touch the same item at the same time, DynamoDB cancels one with the reason `TransactionConflict`. The SDK doesn't retry a cancelled transaction, so your code has to. A busy account that many transfers touch at once will see conflicts, so keep transactions small. The AWS docs say the same: don't group writes into a transaction unless correctness needs it.

Next, know what a transaction doesn't promise. Against requests that touch one item (GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem) and against other transactions, it behaves as if it ran alone, at one instant. That's called serializable. Against Query, Scan and BatchGetItem, it's weaker, read-committed. You never see a write from a transaction that failed. But a Query that runs during a transfer can see some of its items changed and others not yet. To read both accounts as they stood at one moment, use `TransactGetItems`.

The indexes, and DynamoDB Streams (a log of the table's changes that other programs can read), get a transaction's changes one by one. So a program reading the stream can't assume the five writes arrive together. And with global tables, copies of one table in several Regions, the promises hold only in the Region where you made the call.

Retries need two guards, at two levels. The first is the client request token. Send the same `TransactWriteItems` with the same `ClientRequestToken` within 10 minutes, and DynamoDB returns success without writing anything again. Change any part of the request under the same token, and it throws `IdempotentParameterMismatchException`. When you don't set a token, the SDK fills in a fresh UUID, a random id, on every call. That covers the SDK's own quick retries of that call. The second guard is the claim item. Say the same transfer comes back an hour later, with a new time on its ledger entries, because a queue (a list of jobs waiting to be done) delivered it twice. That's a new request with a new token. Only the claim's condition stops it, for as long as the claim lives.

Single-table design has limits as well. DeBrie names two cases where he wouldn't use it. One is a new app whose questions aren't known yet, because each new question can mean a new index, or rewriting old items to give them a new key. The other is GraphQL, a way for an app to ask a server for exactly the fields a screen needs, where each field makes its own request anyway. Triples, Datalog and GraphQL, lesson 9 of this track, shows why. For the core of the payments app, whose six questions are written down and stable, use it.

The Partitioning track's lesson on DynamoDB under the hood opens up the machines behind these requests. It shows how a table is cut into partitions, how each one is copied to three availability zones (separate data centres in one Region), and why a partition splits. Everything in this lesson ran on a store that Amazon runs for you. Next, we'll look at a database you run yourself, built on the same shape.

try.title: Send one transaction twice with the same token
steps: Read `ClientTokenDemo.kt`. It sends one transfer three times with the same `ClientRequestToken`: as it is, the same again, then with 40.00 instead of 30.00. The idempotency claim is in the request too, but look at what the second call returns.
Predict A-1001's balance after the second call, and what the third call does.
Run it. Then stop DynamoDB Local: `docker compose -f env/dynamodb.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
```text
first call with the token:        A-1001 = 7000
same request, same token again:   A-1001 = 7000  (success, nothing written)
same token, amount 40.00:         IdempotentParameterMismatchException
```

The second call returns success, not a cancelled transaction. DynamoDB recognises the token and answers as it did the first time, without writing. That's what a caller needs when the first answer got lost on the way back. Change the request under the same token, and DynamoDB refuses it outright. The token is remembered for 10 minutes after the request finishes, which is why the demo makes a fresh one per run. A retry that comes later, or as a new request, is caught by the claim instead.

a.title: one database transaction

compare.note: Both are all or nothing. PostgreSQL, the database of the SQL track, holds a conversation: the session locks rows statement by statement, can read and decide halfway, and commits when it says so. DynamoDB takes the whole transaction in one request. There are no reads in the middle, only conditions that it checks for you, and at most 100 items. In SQL, a unique constraint on `idem_key` plays the part of `attribute_not_exists`, and the `AND balance_minor >= 3000` guard becomes a condition expression. DynamoDB charges two writes per item for all this. PostgreSQL pays in locks, and in one server that has to take every write.

worked.title: Close the gap from Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics: the claim and the payment in one transaction

steps.say: In Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics, `createPayment` made two calls: a conditional put of the claim, then a plain put of the payment. A crash between them leaves a claim with no payment. Every retry is then told that the payment exists, and it doesn't.

Build both writes as actions. The claim keeps its condition from that lesson: no claim yet, or the old one has expired (a claim lives 86,400 seconds, one day). It also asks for `ALL_OLD`, so a failed claim comes back with the winning claim inside. Its payment id goes in an attribute called `forPayment`. An attribute named `paymentId` would put the claim into the `byPayment` index, next to the payment.
steps.code:
val now = cmd.at.epochSecond
val claim = TransactWriteItem.builder().put(
    Put.builder().tableName(table)
        .item(Keys.key(Keys.claim(cmd.idempotencyKey), Keys.CLAIM) + mapOf(
            "type" to Keys.s("CLAIM"), "forPayment" to Keys.s(cmd.paymentId),
            "fingerprint" to Keys.s(cmd.fingerprint()), "expiresAt" to Keys.n(now + 86_400)))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expiresAt < :now")
        .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":now" to Keys.n(now)))
        .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD)
        .build()
).build()
val payment = TransactWriteItem.builder().put(
    Put.builder().tableName(table).item(Keys.paymentItem(
        Payment(cmd.paymentId, cmd.accountId, cmd.merchantId, cmd.amountMinor, cmd.currency, "AUTHORIZED", cmd.at)
    )).build()
).build()

steps.say: Send them together. If the claim's condition fails, the payment isn't written either, and the reason at index 0 carries the live claim. Compare fingerprints, a short summary of the request's contents, as before. The same fingerprint means a true retry; a different one means the key was used for a different payment. Any other reason, such as `TransactionConflict`, goes back to the caller to retry with the same key.
Check what changed. The crash window is gone, and so is the extra read after a failed claim. The bill is higher: two items in a transaction cost two write units each.

drill.title: The debit action from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the `TransactWriteItem` that takes 30.00 from A-1001's PROFILE item, only if the balance covers it, and returns the old item when the condition fails. Use the low-level client's builders, as the Try-its do. Then say in one sentence why the check must live in the condition and not in Kotlin.

answer.src:
val debit = TransactWriteItem.builder().update(
    Update.builder().tableName("payments")
        .key(mapOf("pk" to AttributeValue.fromS("ACCT#A-1001"), "sk" to AttributeValue.fromS("PROFILE")))
        .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt")   // the arithmetic happens on the server
        .conditionExpression("balanceMinor >= :amt")                 // checked against the item as it is now
        .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":amt" to AttributeValue.fromN("3000")))
        .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD)
        .build()
).build()
// A balance read in Kotlin can be stale by the time the write lands; the condition is checked
// in the same step as the update, so two concurrent debits can't both pass it.

recap: Single-table design keeps several kinds of item under one partition key and names their sort keys so that each screen is one unbroken run. `PROFILE` sorts right after `PAY#`, so one backward Query returns the account and its newest payments.

A global secondary index is a second copy of every item that has its key attributes, under another partition and sort key. Each copy costs a write, lags a moment behind the table and can't be read strongly consistently. Its sort key is used from left to right, with no gaps, and since November 2025 it can have up to four attributes.
`TransactWriteItems` applies up to 100 actions on different items, all or nothing. One false condition cancels everything, and `cancellationReasons()` says which action failed, in the order sent.

Put checks in conditions and sums in update expressions, so DynamoDB checks and changes an item in one step. A client request token stops an identical repeat for 10 minutes; a claim item stops any retry that uses the same key.

The limits: a transaction costs two writes per item, cancelled or not, and only one-item requests see it happen at one instant. The key design is rigid too: a new question can mean a new index, or rewriting old items.
closing:
We started with 30.00 that left your account and never reached your friend's, because two requests were saved one at a time. One `TransactWriteItems` puts the debit, the credit, both statement lines and the claim into a single request that happens completely or not at all.

Open one transfer between two of your own accounts in your banking app. You'll find it twice, once in each account's list. Ask what the app would show if only one of those two lines had been written.

Next, we'll meet Cassandra, a free database program built on the same shape, a key with sorted rows under it, and find out why deleting rows there can make reads slower.

quiz.q: Account A-1001's item collection holds `LEDGER#`, `PAY#`, `PROFILE` and `REFUND#` items. You Query `pk = ACCT#A-1001`, backward, `Limit 21`, with no condition on the sort key. Which item comes back first?
options: The PROFILE item, because the account item always comes first
The newest payment, because the read goes backward in time
The oldest ledger entry, because LEDGER# sorts first
The newest refund, because REFUND# sorts last and a backward read starts at the end
quiz.why: A backward Query starts at the largest sort key in the collection. `R` sorts after `P`, so the refunds sit at the end and come out first. The profile comes first only when a `BETWEEN "PAY#" AND "PROFILE"` condition cuts the refunds off. DynamoDB has no idea which item is "the account" or which is newest; only the order of the sort keys counts.

quiz.q: A `TransactWriteItems` request has five actions. The condition on action 0, the debit, is false. What has DynamoDB written?
options: Actions 1 to 4, because only action 0 failed
Nothing, and the cancellation reasons say `ConditionalCheckFailed` at index 0 and `None` for the rest
Nothing yet: the SDK retries the transaction until the condition holds
Action 0 with its old value, and actions 1 to 4 as sent
quiz.why: One false condition cancels the whole transaction, so no action is applied. The exception's list of reasons has one entry per action, in the order sent, so you can tell which one failed. The SDK doesn't retry a cancelled transaction; your code decides what to do next.

quiz.q: A shop's dashboard queries the `byMerchant` index a few milliseconds after a payment was written to the table, and the payment is missing. What's going on, and what helps?
options: The index is updated a moment after the table; the payment shows up shortly, and only a read of the table is strongly consistent
Set `ConsistentRead` to true on the index Query
The write must have failed without an error; write the payment again
byMerchant is sparse, so it never holds payments
quiz.why: DynamoDB copies table writes into a global secondary index asynchronously, a moment after the write, so an index read can briefly miss a write the table already has. `ConsistentRead` is the tempting fix, but DynamoDB refuses it on an index: "Consistent reads are not supported on global secondary indexes". The index is sparse only for items without `merchantId`, and payments have one.

quiz.q: A transfer is one `TransactWriteItems` with five items, each under 1 KB. Its debit condition fails. How many write units does it use?
options: 0, because nothing was written
5, one per item
10: two per item, prepare and commit, charged even when cancelled
10 if it commits, 5 if it's cancelled
quiz.why: DynamoDB does two writes underneath for every item in a transaction, one to prepare and one to commit, and the AWS docs say they're charged even when the transaction is cancelled. "Nothing was written" is about the data, not the bill.

quiz.q: From Model the access patterns first: `byMerchant` has partition key `merchantId` and sort key `status`, then `createdAt`. A Query asks for `merchantId = M-0042 AND createdAt > 09:00`, any status. What does DynamoDB do?
options: Reads one slice of M-0042's partition, because `createdAt` is part of the sort key
Refuses the Query: `status` comes first in the sort key and has no `=` condition
Runs one Query per status and merges the results
Scans the table and filters by shop and time
quiz.why: The sort key's attributes are used from left to right, with no gaps. The items are sorted by status first, so the payments after 09:00 are spread across every status's run. With a multi-attribute index key, DynamoDB refuses the Query outright: "RANGE key attributes status must have equality conditions specified in the query". It never splits the question into one Query per status on its own.

flashcards.front: Why name the account item `PROFILE` rather than `META`?
flashcards.back: `PROFILE` sorts right after every `PAY#` key (`PA` before `PR`), so a backward Query from `PROFILE` returns the account first and then the newest payments, in one request.

flashcards.front: What puts an item into a global secondary index?
flashcards.back: Having all of the index's key attributes. Items without them are left out, which makes the index sparse.

flashcards.front: Can you read a global secondary index strongly consistently?
flashcards.back: No. DynamoDB updates the index a moment after the table and refuses `ConsistentRead` on it. Read the table when you must see every write.

flashcards.front: What are the limits of one `TransactWriteItems`?
flashcards.back: Up to 100 actions on up to 100 different items, in one AWS account and Region, at most 4 MB in all. No item twice.

flashcards.front: What do a cancelled transaction's reasons tell you?
flashcards.back: One entry per action, in the order sent: `None`, or a code such as `ConditionalCheckFailed` or `TransactionConflict`. With `ALL_OLD`, the failing item as it was.

flashcards.front: What does a write inside a transaction cost?
flashcards.back: Two writes underneath per item, one to prepare and one to commit, even when the transaction is cancelled.

flashcards.front: Client request token or claim item: which one stops what?
flashcards.back: The token turns an identical repeat within 10 minutes into a success that writes nothing. The claim stops any request that uses the same key, for as long as the claim lives.

terms.plain: All the items that share one partition key, stored together and sorted by their sort keys.
Keeping several kinds of item in one DynamoDB table, with sort keys named so that each question is one Query on one item collection.
A second copy of a table's items under a different partition and sort key, which DynamoDB updates a moment after each write.
An index that holds only the items that have its key attributes, such as payments but not ledger entries.
A group of writes that happen together or not at all. DynamoDB's is `TransactWriteItems`, with up to 100 actions.
A test on an item, such as `balanceMinor >= :amt`, that DynamoDB checks in the same step as the write it guards.
The list inside `TransactionCanceledException`, one entry per action, that says which condition failed or which item collided.
An id sent with `TransactWriteItems` so that DynamoDB answers an identical repeat within 10 minutes without writing again.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who is learning to code asks why the payments app keeps accounts, payments, refunds and ledger entries in one DynamoDB table instead of four, and whether a transfer could be two separate updates. Explain both.
explain_back.answer: DynamoDB has no joins, so every table a screen reads is one more request. In one table, an account's items share one partition key and sit together, sorted by sort key, and the keys are named so that each screen is one unbroken run. The account item is called PROFILE so that it sorts right after the payments, and one backward Query returns the account and its 20 newest payments. Questions that don't know the account, such as a payment by id or a shop's failed payments, get a global secondary index: a second copy of the same items under another key, which costs extra writes and lags a moment behind. The price is a table you can't read without the key design next to it. As for the transfer: two updates are two separate requests, each saved on its own, so a crash between them loses the money. One TransactWriteItems puts the debit with its balance condition, the credit, both ledger entries and the idempotency claim into one request. DynamoDB applies all of it or none of it, and tells us which condition failed. It costs two writes per item, so we keep transactions to the writes that must happen together.

deeper.body:
Before multi-attribute keys, single-table designs often used index overloading. Every item got two plain attributes, `gsi1pk` and `gsi1sk`, and each kind of item filled them with something different. A payment put `MERCH#M-0042` and `FAILED#2026-11-07T09:40:27Z` there, a refund put its payment id there, and so on. One index then served several access patterns, at the price of a key design that only a table of item types can explain. You'll meet it in older code and in DeBrie's writing. Since November 2025, with up to four attributes in each half of an index key, you can often name the real attributes instead. Each index still costs its own write on every item it holds, so one overloaded index can still be cheaper than three separate ones.

`TransactGetItems` is the read side: up to 100 Get actions that DynamoDB answers as one consistent snapshot, all the items as they stood at one moment. Use it for a statement that must show both sides of a transfer in the same state. A Query of one collection is only read-committed against transactions, so it could show the debit's new balance next to a page of ledger entries from before.

A transaction that hits a busy item can conflict, or be throttled (slowed down because the table is over its capacity). The right retry is the same request with the same idempotency key, after a short, random wait. Because the SDK fills a fresh client token into every call it makes, a retry that you code yourself is a new request to DynamoDB, and the claim item is what makes it safe.

DynamoDB Streams, the table's change log, records a transaction's item changes as separate records, possibly mixed with other writes. A program that rebuilds balances from the stream should group the records by `transferId` and not assume the five arrive together.
